498.title: Vishvamitra takes the boys
498.hook: a king promises a visitor anything, then hears what he wants
498.howItsDone: Vishvamitra is honored in Hindu tradition as one of the great rishis; the Gayatri mantra of the Rig Veda is traditionally credited to him, and his request for Rama is told as the moment the prince's life of service begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday: payasa from the fire, and four sons born to answer Ravana's boast.
screen: `FOUR SONS, BORN TO ANSWER A BOAST.`

segments.voice: The four princes grow up learned, brave and close. Lakshmana sticks to Rama like a second shadow; Shatrughna to Bharata. Dasharatha, delighted, is already talking with his counselors about their weddings. Then a guard rushes in: the sage Vishvamitra is at the gate. Dasharatha hurries out, washes his feet, honors him, and says the words a king says to an honored guest, and maybe shouldn't: whatever you ask, consider it done. Vishvamitra smiles, and asks.
screen: `FOUR PRINCES, GROWN.` → `A FAMOUS SAGE AT THE GATE.` → `WHATEVER YOU ASK, IT'S DONE.`

segments.voice: Vishvamitra explains. He's begun a sacrifice, and two rakshasas, Maricha and Subahu, keep wrecking it, pouring blood and flesh on the altar. Under his vow he can't curse them in anger. So he asks for Rama. Give me your eldest son, the boy who still wears a child's side-locks, for ten nights, to guard my rite. Dasharatha's world tilts. He nearly faints. Then he pleads, and Valmiki gives us his words: unashodasha-varsho me ramo rajivalochanah. My lotus-eyed Rama is not yet sixteen. He's never fought. Take my army instead. Take me. I'll fight them myself. And when he hears who stands behind Maricha and Subahu, he grows more frightened still: Ravana. No, not Rama. Now, who is Vishvamitra? He wasn't born a sage. He was born a king, a warrior who, the Ramayana tells later, spent ages of fierce austerity until he became a brahmarshi, a sage of the highest rank. His name means friend of the whole world. And he's famous for his fire. When Dasharatha takes back his promise, that fire rises. You're breaking your word, king, he says. Fine. I'll go as I came. And the whole earth, the text says, trembles. Under the noise is something quiet: a father who has promised his son away, and can't bear to let him go.
screen: `TWO RAKSHASAS RUIN HIS SACRIFICE.` · `RAMA IS NOT YET SIXTEEN.` · `A KING WHO BECAME A SAGE.` · `A PROMISE TAKEN BACK.` · then, large: `ŪNAṢOḌAŚAVARṢO ME RĀMO RĀJĪVALOCANAḤ.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you love who is stepping into something bigger than you'd like, a child, a friend, maybe your younger self, and notice if part of you wants to hold on. On each breath out, loosen your grip by one finger: not letting go, just loosening. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer.
Vishvamitra, friend of the whole world. The king-turned-sage asks Dasharatha for Rama to guard his sacrifice, and a father's promise meets a father's fear.
Your line: Rama is not yet sixteen. A promise made, and a father's fear. See you tomorrow.

499.title: Vishvamitra takes the boys
499.hook: the verse that wakes Rama on his first morning away from home is still sung at dawn
499.howItsDone: The Venkatesha Suprabhatam, sung at dawn at the Tirumala temple and played in many homes, opens with Vishvamitra's verse from the Bala Kanda waking Rama.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vishvamitra asked for Rama, a father pleaded, and the sage's anger shook the earth. Your line was Rama is not yet sixteen.

In many homes and temples in South India, the day starts with a recording of a Sanskrit hymn, the Venkatesha Suprabhatam, a song to wake the Lord at Tirupati. Its very first verse isn't new. It's borrowed, word for word, from the Ramayana: what Vishvamitra says to wake Rama on his first morning away from home, sleeping on grass by a river. But first, the boys have to leave.
screen: `A HYMN AT DAWN IN SOUTH INDIA.` → `ITS FIRST VERSE IS FROM THE RAMAYANA.` → `RAMA'S FIRST MORNING AWAY.`

segments.voice: Vasishtha, the royal priest, speaks to the frightened king. You've given your word, he says. Breaking it would undo all your merit. And Vishvamitra knows every divine weapon there is; Rama will be safer with him than anywhere. Dasharatha yields. He calls for Rama, and Lakshmana, who won't be left behind, and blesses them. The boys walk out after the sage, bows in hand, quivers on their backs, and the text says a soft breeze blew and flowers fell from the sky. After a day's walk, on the south bank of the Sarayu, Vishvamitra teaches Rama two mantras, bala and atibala, strength and great strength. With these, he says, you won't feel hunger or thirst or tiredness, and no one will match you, awake or asleep. That night the princes sleep on grass, like ordinary travelers. At dawn the sage wakes them: kausalya supraja rama purva sandhya pravartate, uttishtha narashardula kartavyam daivam ahnikam. Rama, fortunate son of Kausalya, the morning twilight is here. Rise, tiger among men; the day's sacred duties are waiting. The boys rise, bathe, say their prayers and walk on, to a hermitage where, the sage tells them, Shiva once burned Kama, the god of desire, to ash. They've left their father's house. Their teacher's world has begun.

Your line: rise, tiger among men. The sage wakes him by name, gently, with the day's good work waiting. Day four hundred ninety-nine, done.

500.title: Tataka
500.hook: a forest that used to be farmland, and the story of who emptied it
500.howItsDone: Tataka's story is told in Ramayana recitations and in Ramlila performances as the young Rama's first test; some teachers pause on Rama's question and Vishvamitra's answer as a lesson about the duty to protect.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the boys left home, learned bala and atibala, and woke to a sage's dawn verse. Your line was rise, tiger among men. And today's number is worth a pause: five hundred days.

The three travelers cross the Ganga where the Sarayu pours into it, and Rama hears the roar of the two rivers meeting. On the far side, the land changes. A dark, thick forest. No paths. Crickets, harsh birdcalls, lions, tigers, boars, elephants. Nobody lives here. What is this place, Rama asks. The sage's answer surprises him. Not long ago, these were two rich farming lands, full of people and harvests. Someone emptied them.
screen: `WHERE TWO RIVERS MEET.` → `A FOREST WITH NO PATHS.` → `IT USED TO BE FARMLAND.`

segments.voice: Her name is Tataka. She was born a yakshi, a nature spirit, daughter of a yaksha named Suketu, who prayed for a child and was given a daughter with the strength of a thousand elephants. She married Sunda and had a son, Maricha: the same Maricha who has been ruining Vishvamitra's sacrifice. When her husband died, Tataka and her son attacked the great sage Agastya, and Agastya cursed them both. Maricha became a rakshasa. Tataka lost her beauty and became a terrible devourer, and since then she has turned this whole country into wilderness. For the good of the land and everyone who should be living here, the sage says, she has to be stopped. By you. Rama stops. Valmiki lets him ask a real question, and it matters that he does. She's a woman. How can a woman have such strength? The sage, knowing what Rama is really asking, makes his case before Rama acts. Rulers have a duty to protect. When anyone, man or woman, is destroying the lives of others, the protector cannot step back. He gives examples from the old stories, where even the gods acted against women who meant the world harm. It's a hard teaching, and the text doesn't hide that it's hard. A young prince, outside the walls for the first time, is asked to do something that goes against his upbringing. Tomorrow, what he decides.
screen: `FARMLAND TURNED TO WILDERNESS.` · `A YAKSHI, CURSED BY AGASTYA.` · `RAMA STOPS AND ASKS.` · `THE PROTECTOR CANNOT STEP BACK.` · then, large: `TĀṬAKĀ.`

segments.voice: Five hundred days; let that land for a breath. Then picture a place that was once full of life and went quiet, a closed shop, an empty field, a friendship gone dry, and breathe toward it, not to fix it, just to remember what it was and hold the hope that what's empty can be lived in again.
Tataka. The yakshi, cursed by Agastya, who turned two rich lands into wilderness, and whom Vishvamitra asks Rama to stop.
Your line: Rama stops and asks. Valmiki gives him room for a real question first. Day five hundred, and counting.

501.title: Tataka
501.hook: Rama decides, and tries the gentlest way first
501.howItsDone: In Ramayana recitation and performance, Tataka's defeat is told as Rama's first act of protecting the land; commentators and modern readers discuss it in different ways, and some draw attention to Rama's reluctance.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a forest that used to be farmland, a yakshi under a curse, and Rama's real question. Your line was Rama stops and asks.

Rama has listened, and his answer isn't a simple yes. My father told me to do whatever you say, he tells the sage. So I'll do this, for the sake of the cows, the sages and the land. He's acting from obedience, from a promise, not from appetite for a fight. Then he lifts his bow and twangs the string. The sound rolls through the forest. And from deep in the trees, something hears it and comes running.
screen: `MY FATHER TOLD ME TO OBEY YOU.` → `THE TWANG OF THE BOWSTRING.` → `SOMETHING COMES RUNNING.`

segments.voice: Tataka charges out, raising clouds of dust, hurling rocks. Valmiki slows down here. Rama doesn't try to kill her. I'll just take away her power to harm, he tells Lakshmana; I don't want to take her life. He shoots and cuts off her arms. Lakshmana wounds her face. That should end it. It doesn't. Tataka uses her magic, turns invisible, changes shape, and rains stones on them from the air. Enough mercy, Rama, Vishvamitra calls. Evening is coming, and at dusk rakshasas grow stronger. So Rama, tracking her by sound, looses an arrow, and Tataka falls. The gods appear and praise Rama, Vishvamitra embraces him and kisses his head, and the forest, the text says, is freed and becomes beautiful again. How do people read this scene? Traditional teachers see Rama's first act of protection, a land given back to the people meant to live in it, and they point to how hard he tried not to kill. Some modern readers find it painful, a young man pressed to kill a woman, and read the story with that discomfort in view. Both readings take the text seriously. What the text itself makes plain is the order of things. He asked first. He obeyed a promise. He tried to disarm before he destroyed. Only when that failed did he finish it.

502.title: the weapons
502.hook: the morning after the forest is freed, the sage hands over everything he has
502.howItsDone: In the epics, astras are given by teachers or gods to those judged worthy, invoked by mantra; Hindu storytellers often use the gift to Rama to teach that power should follow character.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama obeyed a promise, tried to disarm before he destroyed, and the forest was freed. Your line was disarm before he destroyed.

They spend the night in the freed forest. In the morning, Vishvamitra is smiling. He has watched this boy ask before acting, obey without sulking, try mercy before force. Now the sage decides to hand over everything he has. Not land, not gold. Something no treasury holds, and no army could take from him. Sit down, he tells Rama, and get ready.
screen: `THE SAGE HAS BEEN WATCHING.` → `MERCY BEFORE FORCE.` → `NOW, EVERYTHING HE HAS.`

segments.voice: What Vishvamitra gives are the astras, the divine weapons. An astra isn't just an arrow. It's a power called up by a mantra and released through a weapon: the force of a god, carried on a word. The sage names them one after another, and the list runs on for verses. The discus of dharma and the discus of time. Indra's thunderbolt. Shiva's trident. The weapon of Brahma himself. The noose of Varuna, lord of the waters. The fire weapon, the wind weapon, and one called manava, named for Manu, the first human. As he recites, the weapons appear. Not as metal, but as shining beings with bodies of their own, standing before Rama with palms joined. We are yours, they say. Tell us what to do. Rama, still a young man, touches each one with his hand and answers simply: stay in my mind, and come when I need you. So the weapons aren't things. They're servants with their own presence, and they bow to a person, not just a skill. And look when they're given. Not on day one, but after a test, once the sage has seen how this young man uses force when it's put in his hands. In the Ramayana, power follows character. It doesn't come first.

segments.voice: Think of one strength you have, a skill, a voice people listen to, money, patience, quickness with words, and picture it standing before you, palms joined, waiting. Don't send it anywhere; ask it, the way Rama did, to stay in your mind and come when it's truly needed.

503.title: the weapons
503.hook: a teenager with the gods' weapons asks the one question that matters next
503.carry: teach me to call them back
503.howItsDone: Traditional teachers often point to Rama's request for the withdrawals of the weapons as a sign of his character: a wise person learns how to stop a power before using it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: divine powers stood before Rama as shining beings, and he asked them to stay in his mind. Your line was stay in my mind.

Hand someone the keys to something enormous and listen to their first question. A new driver with a fast car. A new manager with the power to fire people. An eighteen-year-old with a credit card. It's nearly always: what can this do? How fast, how far, how much? Rama has just been handed the weapons of the gods. And walking on through the forest, he asks Vishvamitra something quieter, and wiser.
screen: `THE KEYS TO SOMETHING ENORMOUS.` → `THE USUAL QUESTION: WHAT CAN IT DO?` → `RAMA ASKS ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: I've received the weapons, Rama says, and even the gods would find them hard to overcome. Now teach me how to call them back. In Sanskrit, the release is prayoga; the withdrawal is samhara. Vishvamitra is delighted, and teaches him. Again the powers appear, a whole new company of shining beings with names of their own, palms joined. These are the withdrawals: the knowledge of how to stop what you've started. Rama asks them, too, to come to his mind when he needs them. Why does Valmiki give this a whole moment? Because in the epics, a weapon you can't call back is a disaster, and later there are stories of warriors who could launch a terrible power and not withdraw it. Rama, this young, asks for the brake before he ever touches the accelerator. That's the kind of person the sage has been looking for. The road goes on to a green, peaceful hermitage on a hill, with deer grazing and birds calling. Whose is it, Rama asks. This is Siddhashrama, the sage says. Long ago Vishnu did his austerities here, and it was the hermitage of Vamana, the dwarf, who asked King Bali for three steps of land and crossed the worlds in three strides. My sacrifice is waiting here. And here the weapons will be needed.

504.title: the weapons
504.hook: six nights awake, a silent sage, and an arrow that chooses not to kill
504.carry: a way to walk off whole
504.howItsDone: Ramayana tellings mark Maricha's survival here because he returns in the Aranya Kanda as the golden deer; teachers often point out that Rama chose a weapon that would stun, not kill.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama asked how to call the weapons back, and the sage taught him the withdrawal. Your line was teach me to call them back.

At Siddhashrama, Vishvamitra begins his sacrifice and takes a vow of silence; from now on he can't say a word. So the hermits tell the boys: for six days and six nights, you have to guard him. Rama and Lakshmana stand watch, bows ready, and don't sleep. Five days pass. Nothing. On the sixth, the altar fire suddenly flares up on its own. The sky goes dark. And out of the dark comes a roar, and a rain of blood.
screen: `A VOW OF SILENCE.` → `SIX NIGHTS ON WATCH.` → `THE SIXTH DAY: A RAIN OF BLOOD.`

segments.voice: Maricha and Subahu have come, with their followers, to wreck the rite. Watch this, Rama tells Lakshmana. He takes up the manava weapon, the one named for Manu, the first human, and fires it at Maricha's chest. It doesn't kill him. It lifts him and hurls him a hundred yojanas, far out over the sea, where he falls, stunned, but alive. Rama says it plainly: the manava has knocked him senseless, but it hasn't taken his life. Then the fire weapon for Subahu, who falls dead, and the wind weapon to scatter the rest. The sacrifice is finished. Vishvamitra, his vow complete, says: you've made the name of this place come true. Siddhashrama, the hermitage of accomplishment. Hold onto Maricha. He's still out there, alive, and he'll come back in this story wearing a very different shape. Now the week, from the top. A father's plea that his son isn't yet sixteen. Vasishtha's counsel and the sage's dawn verse. A forest that used to be farmland. Rama asking first, and disarming before destroying. The weapons appearing with joined palms, and how to call them back. And today, the first real use: one enemy spared, and a promise kept.
screen: `THE MANAVA FOR MARICHA.` · `HURLED OVER THE SEA, STILL ALIVE.` · `THE FIRE WEAPON FOR SUBAHU.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `SIDDHASHRAMA: ACCOMPLISHED.`

segments.voice: Sit as if you're on watch, not tense, just awake: eyes low, back long, breath even, noticing each sound arrive and pass the way the boys watched the dark for six nights. If your attention wanders, come back to the watch without scolding yourself.
The weapons. At Siddhashrama, Rama uses them for the first time: the manava hurls Maricha out to sea alive, and the sacrifice is completed.
Your line: a way to walk off whole. Rama chose the weapon that stuns, not the one that kills. A week on the road, complete.
